what_it_does: This paper presents SDISC, a low-power chip that lets a person control a machine in real time using biological signals like muscle activity (EMG — electrical signals from muscles) or brainwaves (EEG — electrical signals from the brain). Instead of processing continuous streams of numbers like a conventional computer, SDISC uses a spiking neural network (SNN) — a type of artificial neural network that only fires when something meaningful changes, similar to how real neurons work. This makes the computation extremely energy-efficient because most of the hardware sits idle most of the time. The math is done directly inside a special type of memory chip called RRAM (resistive RAM — a non-volatile memory that can also multiply numbers), so data never has to travel back and forth to a separate processor. The paper also introduces techniques to compensate for the fact that RRAM cells gradually drift and become less reliable over time.
